statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: Governed under Metropolitan Filaret of Moscow and, later, the state-appointed ober-procurator Konstantin Pobedonostsev. Sent missions to the Altai peoples and to Japan (from 1861, under Nikolai), and reached the 1905 toleration edict that opened the way to the council that restored the patriarchate. The Optina elders' renewal movement grew within this church, and Alaska was one of its missions. It stood in tension with the separate Old Believer Belokrinitsa hierarchy, founded in 1846, and with the evangelical Stundist movement that broke from it.
why: For a century Russia's church had no patriarch of its own, governed instead by a lay official answering to the tsar. Metropolitan Filaret spent decades pushing through a Russian-language Bible against long resistance, finished in 1876, while later the ober-procurator Konstantin Pobedonostsev used the same church to enforce religious uniformity on Old Believers, Eastern Catholics and evangelicals alike.
legacy: The Bible Filaret fought for is still the Russian Orthodox Church's standard translation, and the missionary churches begun in this period — in Japan, in Alaska — are still there. Its deepest legacy is the council it spent the century waiting for. The preparatory work of 1905-06 became the Moscow Council of 1917-18, which restored the patriarchate just as the revolution arrived that would try to destroy it.

name: Armenian Christianity — the Zartonk Century
statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: The Zartonk century produced the Armenian National Constitution of 1863, which gave lay delegates power to limit the Patriarch's authority. Converts of American missionaries were expelled from the Apostolic Church and organized as the Armenian Evangelical Church in 1846, recognized by the Ottoman state as a separate Protestant community in 1850. The century ended in the Hamidian massacres of 1894-96.
why: Because the Ottoman state treated the Armenian church as the legal body of the whole nation, a century of awakening in language, schools and printing ran largely through it. Its 1863 National Constitution gave lay delegates a formal check on the Patriarch's own authority, an unusual arrangement that outlived the massacres of 1894-96 that closed the century in blood.
legacy: The Armenian Apostolic Church remains the national church of Armenia and of a diaspora this century's emigrations began. The Armenian Evangelical Church founded in 1846 and the Armenian Catholic Church are both still here, small and continuous. The habit of lay representation written into the 1863 constitution survived into the Apostolic Church's later governance. And the awakening's institutions — its schools, presses and newspapers — carried a national literature and a national self-understanding that the catastrophe of the following decade would scatter across the world but not extinguish.

name: The Old Catholic Churches — Utrecht to the Union

otherLinksToLivingEntries.otherName: The Catholic Church of the Long Nineteenth Century
The Russian Church — the Synodal Century

statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: Formed when German, Swiss and Austrian Catholics rejected the First Vatican Council's definition of papal infallibility. Ignaz von Döllinger was excommunicated in 1871, and Utrecht consecrated Joseph Hubert Reinkens as the first bishop of the German Old Catholics in 1873. In 1889 five bishops signed the Declaration of Utrecht, founding the Union of Utrecht.
why: When German, Swiss and Austrian Catholics refused the pope's new claim to infallibility in 1870, an old Dutch church at Utrecht, out of communion with Rome since an eighteenth-century dispute but still holding valid bishops, consecrated one of their own. The five bishops who signed the 1889 Declaration of Utrecht professed the faith of the undivided church of the first thousand years, then dropped required celibacy for priests and put the liturgy into the language of the people.
legacy: The Union of Utrecht is still there. It is a small family of national churches in the Netherlands, Germany, Switzerland, Austria, Poland and the Czech lands. Its most lasting work turned out to be ecumenical. In 1874 and 1875 Dollinger called meetings at Bonn that brought Old Catholic, Anglican and Orthodox theologians to one table. Their theses were a first attempt to set down the faith all three held in common. In 1931 the Old Catholics and the Church of England entered full communion by the Bonn Agreement.

name: Nineteenth-Century Methodism
statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: British Wesleyan Methodism consolidated into a settled denomination. The Primitive Methodists formed after the 1807 Mow Cop camp meeting, becoming a settled connexion by 1811-12, known for their women itinerant preachers and working-class base. In America, the Methodist family split into northern and southern churches in 1844 over slavery, after Black Methodists had already formed their own churches, the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1816 and the AME Zion Church in 1821.
why: Methodism split repeatedly as it grew. In Britain, working-class converts who found the Wesleyan church too respectable formed the Primitive Methodists after an 1807 camp meeting, sending women itinerant preachers into the pit villages, while in America, Black Methodists refused equal standing built their own churches, the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1816 and the AME Zion Church in 1821, years before slavery split the wider American church in two.
legacy: Methodism became one of the largest Protestant families in the world: the United Methodist Church and British Methodism, the AME, AME Zion and CME churches, and Methodist churches across Africa and Asia all descend from this century's expansion. Its machinery outlasted it too — the class meeting, the itinerant preacher, the connexional conference. So did its conviction that holiness is meant to be practical and available now, which passed through the Holiness movement into Pentecostalism and from there into a very large share of world Christianity.

name: Nineteenth-Century Baptists
statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: Spurgeon preached to thousands each week at the Metropolitan Tabernacle in London. In 1845 the split over slavery gave birth to the Southern Baptist Convention. Landmarkism traced an unbroken line of true Baptist churches back to the apostles. Late in the century Spurgeon left the Baptist Union. He called the fight the Down-Grade. He was sure his fellow ministers were giving up old truths.
why: Baptists never agreed to be governed from anywhere. Yet in London one preacher, Charles Haddon Spurgeon, drew thousands each week and sold his printed sermons by the million. Late in life he broke with the Baptist Union over what he called the Down-Grade. He was sure his fellow ministers were quietly giving up what they had been ordained to preach. Forty years before, in 1845, American Baptists had split. Southern churches had been refused when they put forward a slaveholder as a missionary.
legacy: The bodies formed in this century are still the shape of Baptist life. The Southern Baptist Convention became the largest Protestant denomination in the United States. The Baptist Union of Great Britain and its sister bodies carry on. Spurgeon's sermons have never gone out of print. Two older Baptist lines also ran on through these years. The Black Baptist churches of America go back to the 1770s. William Carey's Baptist mission society was founded in 1792. In his own call for it, Carey said no one had matched the Moravians as missionaries.

name: Nineteenth-Century Quakerism — the Separations
statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: The Hicksite separation of 1827–28 was the defining split of the century for the Society of Friends. It was followed by a further division between the evangelical Gurneyite and conservative Wilburite wings, and by a pastoral-system revival that introduced planned worship and paid ministers to part of the movement.
why: Friends split first in 1827-28 over Elias Hicks' teaching that the Inward Light, not the Bible or a doctrine of atonement, stood at the heart of the faith, then split again between evangelical and conservative wings. Out of the evangelical stream came something Quakers had never had before: revival meetings, planned worship, and paid pastors, so that by the century's end some meetings sat in silence while others sang hymns and listened to sermons.
legacy: All three streams are still here: the pastoral, evangelical Friends who are now the majority of Quakers worldwide — most of them in Kenya and Latin America. The unprogrammed liberal meetings, and the small conservative bodies that kept the older ways. Friends' public work outlasted their divisions. The peace testimony survived the separations intact, the relief agencies that grew from it were jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1947, and the Quaker practice of seeking the sense of a meeting rather than counting votes has been borrowed far outside the Society.

name: American Unitarianism & Universalism — the Consolidations
statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: In 1819 William Ellery Channing gave a sermon in Baltimore. It set out what the liberals held, and it spoke out against the Trinity. On 25 May 1825 they formed the American Unitarian Association. The Universalists built their conventions on a track of their own. A third strain went further still. The Transcendentalists left more Christian doctrine behind than most of their elders would.
why: The Universalists built their movement on a single conviction, that God would in the end save everyone, while the Unitarians organized around William Ellery Channing's 1819 sermon and an explicit rejection of the Trinity. A generation later, Ralph Waldo Emerson pushed further still, leaving the pulpit to tell Harvard's divinity students in 1838 to seek religion in intuition and nature rather than historical revelation.
legacy: Both bodies survived, and in 1961 merged into the Unitarian Universalist Association, still a functioning denomination in North America. Their wider mark is out of proportion to their numbers. The Transcendentalists' essays became a permanent part of American literature, and the causes the movement threw itself into — abolition, public education, humane treatment of prisoners and the mentally ill. Long outlived the theological arguments that produced them.

name: The Ruthenian Greek Catholic Church — Polotsk to Galicia

otherLinksToLivingEntries.otherName: The Russian Church — the Synodal Century

statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: The Synod of Polotsk in 1839 dissolved the union with Rome across the Russian Empire, transferring roughly a million and a half people to Russian Orthodoxy; the Chełm eparchy followed in 1875. The church survived only under Austrian rule in Galicia, where it became the institutional engine of Ukrainian national life, especially under Metropolitan Andrey Sheptytsky from 1900. It stood in natural tension with the Russian Orthodox Church, which absorbed the dissolved dioceses.
why: At the Synod of Polotsk in 1839, bishops declared their church reunited with Russian Orthodoxy and roughly a million and a half Eastern-rite Catholics were transferred by decree; a further eparchy followed in 1875, some of it by force. Under Austrian rule in Galicia the church survived instead, its priests doubling as the schoolteachers, editors and cooperative organizers of a Ukrainian people who had almost no other leadership of their own.
legacy: The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church is the largest Eastern Catholic church in the world today. All it survived later rested on the base it built in Galicia in this century: Soviet liquidation in 1946, four decades underground, and its return to the open in 1989. In the lands where the union was ended by decree, it never came back. The church's habit of carrying a national culture as well as a liturgy took shape here. It is still one of the most distinctive things about it.

name: Philippine Catholicism — Gomburza to the Aglipayan Schism

otherLinksToLivingEntries.otherName: The Philippine Independent Church in the Twentieth Century

statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: Grew out of the secularization controversy and the 1872 Gomburza executions, which fed directly into the Philippine independence movement. The Iglesia Filipina Independiente was proclaimed in 1902 as the Spanish colonial-era church question came to a head, and it later adopted a trinitarian Declaration of Faith in 1947.
why: The 1872 garrotting of three priests, Mariano Gomez, Jose Burgos and Jacinto Zamora, remembered together as Gomburza, did more to fuel the independence movement than their campaign for Filipino-run parishes ever had; Jose Rizal dedicated his second novel to their memory. Three decades later a labor organizer, Isabelo de los Reyes, proclaimed an independent Philippine church and put the former revolutionary chaplain Gregorio Aglipay at its head.
legacy: The Iglesia Filipina Independiente is still a functioning church, and since 1961 has been in full communion with the Episcopal Church and the wider Anglican Communion. The Catholic Church it broke from remained the country's majority faith and, over the following decades, got what the secularization campaign had asked for: a Filipino hierarchy drawn from Filipino clergy. Gomburza became a national memory more than a churchly one — three priests' names on monuments and in schoolbooks, taught as the beginning of a country.

name: The Church of the East & the Chaldean Consolidation

otherLinksToLivingEntries.otherName: The Catholic Church of the Long Nineteenth Century

statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: John Hormizd was confirmed as Chaldean patriarch in 1830, consolidating the modern Chaldean Catholic Church as a single body in communion with Rome. The line that stayed independent kept its seat at Qudshanis and became known as the Assyrian Church of the East.
why: This was once a missionary church whose bishops reached from Baghdad as far as China. By the nineteenth century its patriarch lived in a mountain village in Hakkari. A rival line, which Rome recognized in 1830, had become the Chaldean Catholic Church. In 1886 the Archbishop of Canterbury sent a mission to the remaining Assyrian line. He told it to strengthen the old church, not to convert its people.
legacy: Both churches are still here, and both are now largely churches of exile. The Chaldean Catholic Church remains the largest Christian body native to Iraq. The Assyrian Church of the East, driven out of the Hakkari mountains during the First World War, spent most of the twentieth century with its patriarch abroad and only returned the seat to Erbil in 2015. The Urmia press left a quieter legacy: printing Scripture and schoolbooks in the language people actually spoke helped make modern Aramaic a written literary language, which it has remained.

name: The Confessional Lutheran Revival & the Emigrations
statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: In 1817 the Prussian Union forced Lutheran and Reformed churches to merge. Old Lutherans who would not join were hounded, and some left for Australia. In 1838 a separate group of Saxon Lutherans sailed for America. Out of that group came the Missouri Synod in 1847. In Germany the same instinct led to a new school of Lutheran thought at Erlangen. It also drove the work of Wilhelm Löhe at Neuendettelsau.
why: When Prussia's king ordered Lutheran and Reformed churches merged in 1817, some Lutherans chose exile instead. Whole congregations sailed for South Australia rather than give in. A separate group of Saxon Lutherans reached Missouri in the same years. Within months it had to depose its own leader for misconduct. Out of that chastened remnant C. F. W. Walther built the Missouri Synod of 1847. It was a church where you belonged only if you signed the old confessions.
legacy: The churches this produced are on three continents still: the Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod and the Wisconsin Synod in North America, the Lutheran Church of Australia, and the independent Lutheran churches of Germany. Their parochial schools became one of the largest Protestant school systems in the United States. The wider legacy is a pattern rather than an institution. A church defined by a written confession rather than by a state, a nation or a revival, which became one of the standing options in Protestant life and remains an argument Protestants have with each other.

name: Malagasy Christianity — the Self-Carried Church
statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: The London Missionary Society arrived in 1818/1820, and the first baptisms took place in 1831. Queen Ranavalona I banned Christianity in 1835, and Rasalama was martyred in 1837. The church then grew for twenty-five years with no missionaries at all. Ranavalona II converted in 1869, and the French conquest of 1895-96 ended the kingdom that housed the church.
why: Missionaries gave Madagascar's language its first written form and, by 1835, a complete Bible, the same year Queen Ranavalona I banned Christianity outright and drove them out. For the next quarter-century believers had no foreign clergy at all, only the Bible and hymns they had been left, and when missionaries were finally allowed back they found far more Christians than they had left behind.
legacy: Most people in Madagascar are still Christians. The churches grown from this time remain among the island's largest bodies. Four memorial churches stand in the capital, Antananarivo, on the spots where believers were killed. The story also went far beyond the island. Sermons and mission magazines told it again and again in the 1800s. It became their standard example of a church that held together with no clergy and no protection at all.

name: East African Christianity & the Uganda Martyrs

otherLinksToLivingEntries.otherName: The Catholic Church of the Long Nineteenth Century

statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: Johann Ludwig Krapf began mission work on the coast in 1844, and the Universities' Mission to Central Africa followed in 1857. The Church Missionary Society and the Catholic White Fathers reached Buganda in 1877 and 1879. Anglican and Catholic pages together became the Uganda Martyrs, executed between 1885 and 1887, with Charles Lwanga burned at Namugongo in 1886. By the 1900 Agreement that settled Buganda's relations with Britain, it was a Christian kingdom. The revival movement that swept the same churches decades later grew out of this same soil.
why: When the kabaka Mwanga II turned on Buganda's Anglican and Catholic converts in 1885-87, he killed both kinds together, the largest group burned alive at Namugongo under Charles Lwanga, who is said to have arranged his own pyre. The persecution did not stop the faith's spread; Baganda converts carried it outward as evangelists to neighboring kingdoms faster than any mission society could have managed on its own.
legacy: Uganda became one of the most heavily Christian countries in Africa, and the martyrs are honored on both sides of the division that produced them — canonized by the Catholic Church in 1964, commemorated in the Anglican calendar, with shrines of both communions at Namugongo that draw enormous crowds every 3 June. The pattern set here mattered as much as the memory. African Christians carrying the faith to neighboring peoples on their own initiative is how Christianity actually spread across this region, and the revival that swept these same churches from the 1930s grew out of the same soil.

name: The Taiping Heavenly Kingdom

otherLinksToLivingEntries.otherName: The Missionary Movement's Native Churches (Serampore India; Sierra Leone & the Niger; Pacific Islands; China Coast & CIM)

statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: Hong Xiuquan and his cousin Feng Yunshan gathered the God Worshippers in Guangxi. In 1851 they declared the Heavenly Kingdom. They took Nanjing in 1853 and held it until 1864. The war to crush them cost some twenty million lives. It was the largest movement of the century built on Christian ideas, and its worst disaster. It left no church behind. But it left many Chinese wary of Christianity, and later missionaries met that fear everywhere.
why: Hong Xiuquan, a village schoolteacher who had failed China's imperial examinations four times, came to believe after rereading a Christian tract that he was God's second son and the younger brother of Jesus Christ. The kingdom he and his followers built on that conviction banned opium and footbinding, held land in common, and lasted eleven years before the war fought to destroy it killed an estimated twenty million people.
legacy: The Heavenly Kingdom left no church. Its institutions were destroyed with it in 1864 and no continuing body traces its descent from Hong Xiuquan. What it left instead was consequence. The Qing dynasty was permanently weakened by the war and by the regional armies raised to win it; the lower Yangtze countryside took generations to recover. And Chinese officials and villagers alike had been handed a reason to associate Christianity with rebellion and mass death, a suspicion that later missionaries met everywhere they went. Later Chinese revolutionaries, Sun Yat-sen among them, looked back on the Taiping as forerunners, and the movement remains a fixture of Chinese historical memory and museum display.

name: Japanese Christianity — the Hidden Christians’ Emergence & the Meiji Church

otherLinksToLivingEntries.otherName: The Russian Church — the Synodal Century
The Catholic Church of the Long Nineteenth Century

statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: On 17 March 1865, Urakami villagers revealed themselves at Ōura, and roughly 30,000 hidden believers came forward in the months that followed. The Urakami community faced a final persecution until 1873. Some, the Kakure, chose to stay separate from the visible church. Protestant bands grew alongside, including Uchimura Kanzo's Mukyōkai movement founded in 1901, and Nikolai's Russian Orthodox mission dated from 1861.
why: On 17 March 1865 a group of villagers walked into a newly opened church in Nagasaki and quietly told the priest their hearts were the same as his, descendants of Christians driven underground more than two centuries earlier who had kept baptism, prayer and a liturgical calendar with no priest at all. Not everyone who surfaced rejoined the visible church; some, the Kakure, chose to keep the faith exactly as they had received it, and remain separate to this day.
legacy: Christianity in Japan stayed small — roughly one per cent of the population then and now — but its institutions outlasted the century. Doshisha and other mission-founded universities, the Orthodox cathedral in Tokyo that Nikolai built, and a Catholic community around Nagasaki that is still the largest in the country. The hidden Christians' story became the basis of a UNESCO World Heritage listing of Nagasaki-region sites in 2018, and it has had a long literary afterlife, most famously in Endo Shusaku's novel Silence.

name: The Haitian Church — Rupture to Concordat

otherLinksToLivingEntries.otherName: The Catholic Church of the Long Nineteenth Century

statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: Haiti's church was cut off from Rome for the whole time after independence in 1804. Almost no priests trained under Rome arrived, and the state ran the church. In that gap a religious life that joined Catholic and Vodou practice took shape. A concordat signed on 28 March 1860 ended the break.
why: For fifty-six years after independence, Haiti's parishes were served by men of irregular standing, some genuine priests under suspension, some who had simply taken the title, since Rome refused to recognize the new republic at all. In that long vacancy, Catholic sacraments and feast days wove together with Vodou practice inherited from West Africa into a religious life most Haitians have held as one thing rather than two.
legacy: The hierarchy the 1860 concordat established is still the framework of the Haitian Catholic Church, the country's largest institution. The creole religious world formed during the schism is also still there, and the church's relationship to it — stretches of quiet accommodation alternating with campaigns to stamp it out, most violently the anti-superstition drives of the 1940s — has been one of the defining questions of Haitian religion ever since.

name: The Alaskan Mission — Herman’s Decades & Veniaminov

otherLinksToLivingEntries.otherName: The Russian Church — the Synodal Century
American Orthodoxy — Autocephaly & the Convert Wave

statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: Veniaminov reached Unalaska in 1824 and created Aleut and Tlingit alphabets and translations. Herman lived out his last decades as a hermit, dying in 1836. Veniaminov was made bishop, taking the name Innocent, in 1840. After Russia sold Alaska in 1867, the church stayed on as a native church under its own Alaska Native clergy.
why: Herman, a hermit monk on Spruce Island, spent his last decades fighting the Russian trading company over its treatment of the Alutiiq children in the school and orphanage he ran for them. Ioann Veniaminov, arriving at nearby Unalaska in 1824, gave Aleut its first alphabet and translated Scripture into it, and when Russia sold Alaska in 1867 and went home, the church he helped build stayed on, kept alive by Alaska Native clergy in their own languages.
legacy: Orthodoxy is still a living Alaska Native tradition, with dozens of parishes serving villages across the Aleutians, the Kodiak archipelago and the Yukon-Kuskokwim delta, many of them keeping services in Yup'ik, Aleut and Tlingit alongside English. The mission also became the root of Orthodoxy in North America as a whole. The diocese Veniaminov founded moved its seat to San Francisco and then to New York, and is the ancestor of today's Orthodox Church in America. Herman's grave on Spruce Island is still a place of pilgrimage.

name: Nineteenth-Century Latin American Catholicism

otherLinksToLivingEntries.otherName: The Catholic Church of the Long Nineteenth Century

statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: Independence brought the patronato fights and Rome's slow recognition of the new governments. Liberal and clerical factions clashed, most sharply in Mexico's Reforma. Rome pursued the Romanization of the continent's church, culminating in the 1899 Latin American Plenary Council. Brazil's imperial church faced its own conflicts with the state.
why: When Spanish America's new republics claimed the same right to appoint bishops the Spanish crown once held, Rome took a generation to recognize either the governments or their nominees, leaving dioceses vacant and seminaries shut. Mexico's Reform laws stripped the church of its property in the 1850s and Brazil imprisoned two of its own bishops in the 1870s, while ordinary Catholics kept their confraternities, patronal feasts and household saints going with far fewer priests than Europe had.
legacy: This is the century that made Latin America's church what it is: a Roman-aligned hierarchy laid over a much older popular Catholicism, with far fewer priests per head than Europe had, and a long habit of arguing with the state. The 1899 council in Rome was the first time the continent's bishops met as a single body. They met again as a continent at Rio in 1955 and at Medellin in 1968. Latin America is still home to the largest share of the world's Catholics.

name: Ethiopian Christianity — Tewodros to Menelik

otherLinksToLivingEntries.otherName: The Coptic Revival — Cyril IV and After

statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: Tewodros II ruled from 1855 to 1868. Yohannes IV settled the Tewahedo doctrinal question at the Council of Boru Meda in 1878. Menelik II won the decisive victory over Italy at Adwa in 1896.
why: Tewodros II seized church lands and tried to bring the clergy under his own control, a quarrel that ended with a British army at Magdala and his suicide in 1868. A decade later Yohannes IV settled a two-century theological argument over how Christ's divinity and humanity are united at the Council of Boru Meda, even as the church that ruling bound together still had to receive its own head, the abun, from the Coptic patriarch in Egypt.
legacy: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church is one of the largest of the ancient Oriental Orthodox churches, and both things this century settled are still in place: the Tewahedo doctrine ruled at Boru Meda, and the independence Adwa secured. The one arrangement that did change came later — the church received its first Ethiopian bishops in 1929 and its own patriarch in 1959, ending sixteen centuries of taking its head from Alexandria. Adwa itself became a byword far beyond Ethiopia, a rallying point for Pan-Africanism and, in the Caribbean and the Americas, for movements that looked to Ethiopia as the image of an Africa that had never been conquered.

name: Dutch Neo-Calvinism & the Secession Churches
statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: The Afscheiding secession of 1834 led American emigrants to found the Christian Reformed Church in North America in 1857. Abraham Kuyper led a second secession, the Doleantie, in 1886, founded the Free University in 1880, and brought the two streams together in the 1892 union that formed the Gereformeerde Kerken in Nederland.
why: When Hendrik de Cock's congregation walked out of the Dutch national church in 1834, the state fined them and billeted soldiers on them for holding illegal services. Fifty years later Abraham Kuyper led a second, larger secession on a bigger idea, that Christ's claim covers every sphere of life, each with its own proper authority, and built a university, a newspaper and a political party to carry it out rather than withdraw from society or dissolve into it.
legacy: The churches are still here: the Dutch Reformed families at home, most of them since 2004 inside the Protestant Church in the Netherlands, and in North America the Christian Reformed Church with its schools and colleges. Kuyper's larger idea traveled furthest. Sphere sovereignty and a Christian worldview applied to scholarship, politics and the arts became a standing tradition in Reformed thought and shaped a great deal of evangelical higher education in North America. It also traveled in a direction Kuyper's heirs still argue about, supplying vocabulary that South African theologians later adapted in defense of apartheid.

name: Russian Evangelicals — Stundists to the Baptist Union

otherLinksToLivingEntries.otherName: The Russian Church — the Synodal Century
The Russian Church — the Synodal Century
Persecuted-Church Traditions of the Communist Era (Initsiativniki Baptists; Romania's Lord's Army)

statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: It grew from two roots. In the 1860s Ukrainian peasants began to meet to study the Bible, and their neighbors called them Stundists. From 1874 a second circle met in St Petersburg around Vasily Pashkov. Their leaders met in 1884 to unite, but the police broke up the meeting. That year the Baptist churches of the south formed a Russian Baptist Union, while Pashkov's followers stayed apart. Konstantin Pobedonostsev, the lay official who ran the Orthodox Church for the tsar, led the state's campaign against them. They had left that church, and to leave it was a crime. Their churches are the ancestors of the Soviet-era Initsiativniki Baptists.
why: Ukrainian peasants working alongside German colonists in the 1860s began holding Bible study meetings their neighbors called Stunden, hours, and read Russia's own new translation of Scripture for themselves. A decade later, a guards colonel named Vasily Pashkov opened his St Petersburg house to preaching that servants and nobles attended side by side, a movement the state answered with exile, broken-up meetings and children taken from their parents, since leaving the Orthodox Church was a crime as well as a sin.
legacy: These congregations are the ancestors of Russian and Ukrainian evangelical Protestantism as it now exists. The Baptist and Evangelical Christian unions descended from them survived the Soviet century, went through their own painful split in the 1960s between those who registered with the state and those who refused, and are today, with the Pentecostals, the largest Protestant presence across the former Soviet Union. Emigrants carried the tradition abroad as well, into Slavic Baptist communities in North and South America and Germany that are still identifiably from this root.

name: Azusa Street & Early Pentecostalism

livingEvidence.basis: An episode or window of a living tradition. The mission closed in 1931 and the revival is an episode. The mark rests on the tradition it began, as eras 1 to 9 mark an episode of a living tradition (VIII.5, Oxford Movement, 1833-1906, living).
livingEvidence.evidence: World Christian Encyclopedia, 3rd ed. (2019): independent counter for the Pentecostal family, cited at IX.11 and IX.15; verified; Pew, Global Christianity (Dec 2011): independent survey; verified; Anderson, An Introduction to Pentecostalism, 2nd ed. (2013/14): survey scholarship; verified; Espinosa, William J. Seymour (2014): history of the revival; [S].
livingEvidence.grade: CD (Contemporary-Documented); newest dated item 2019, newest verified 2019

otherLinksToLivingEntries.otherName: The Black Church in the Twentieth Century

statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a self-documenting record — the mission's own paper The Apostolic Faith, Seymour's 1915 Doctrines and Discipline, and participants' memoirs read beside the hostile press file. Its window closes in the 1920s: the mission's decline after 1909 and Seymour's death in 1922 close this episode, not the movement, which went on long after it.
relationsSummary: It grew out of the Holiness movement and Black church worship. Many of this era's Pentecostal churches trace their line back to it. Others, such as Africa's prayer churches, began with their own leaders.
why: The revival broke out on Azusa Street in Los Angeles in April 1906. It grew from two streams already flowing together, Holiness worship and Black church worship. It spread not by hierarchy but by print. The mission's own newspaper, The Apostolic Faith, went out free and started meetings in places its founders never visited. Local papers mocked it as a "Weird Babel of Tongues." William Seymour kept leading the mission until his death in 1922. Many Pentecostal churches of the twentieth century traced their line back to what happened on that street.
legacy: The revival's own episode closed in the 1920s, but the tradition it started did not. Many movements in this era's Pentecostal family run back through here. Scholars still argue over how far the Global South churches and Africa's independent churches do. New church bodies formed fast. The Church of God in Christ turned Pentecostal in 1907, and the Assemblies of God was formed in 1914. In 1913 a quarrel over the doctrine of God broke out inside the same young movement. It gave rise to Oneness Pentecostalism. What traveled furthest was not a doctrine but a way of meeting: testimony, song, and the expectation that anyone present might speak.

name: The 1904-07 Revival Family (Wales; Mukti India; Pyongyang Korea)

livingEvidence.basis: An episode or window of a living tradition. The wave subsided c. 1910. The mark would rest on the churches it left, with no dated present-day source for any of them.
livingEvidence.evidence: No dated source after 2010 attests the Welsh, Indian or Korean churches the revivals left; Oak, The Making of Korean Christianity (2013): history of 1876-1915; [S].
livingEvidence.grade: none (no dated item after 2010 is in the repo)

otherLinksToLivingEntries.otherName: Korean Protestantism in the Twentieth Century

statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on journalists' and missionaries' near-verbatim records of three revivals that broke out independently. Its window ends in 1910 — the wave subsided, but the churches it left behind did not — and the Korean origin lines belong on this row too.
relationsSummary: These revivals arose independently of the Azusa Street revival happening around the same time, rather than descending from it — revival broke out in more than one place at once. Korea's revival grew out of earlier missionary and indigenous groundwork: Horace Allen's arrival in 1884, Underwood and Appenzeller in 1885, the Nevius method adopted in 1890, and Sŏ Sang-yun's earlier work distributing scripture.
why: Revival broke out almost at once in three unconnected places -- Wales in 1904, the Mukti mission in India in 1905, and a Bible conference in Pyongyang in 1907 -- and none of the three descended from the others or from Azusa Street. Journalists and missionaries recorded each one nearly as it happened, from the Western Mail's daily reports on Wales to Minnie Abrams's account of Mukti, leaving three separate beginnings rather than one single source.
legacy: The wave subsided around 1910; the churches did not. Korea's church in particular grew out of this decade and the decades just before it — Horace Allen's arrival in 1884, Underwood and Appenzeller in 1885, the Nevius method adopted in 1890 — and it went on growing long after the revival wave had passed. The three revivals together are the standing argument that revival is polygenetic: it broke out in unconnected places at nearly the same time, which is a harder and more honest fact than any single point of origin. The journalism, the mission presses and the Korean church's own histories they generated are the record.

name: The East African Revival (Balokole)

livingEvidence.basis: An episode or window of a living tradition. The wave subsided by the 1970s. The 2012 studies are verified, but the repo does not say they describe the fellowships as still meeting.
livingEvidence.evidence: Peterson (2012) and Ward & Wild-Wood, The East African Revival: History and Legacies (2012): independent scholarship; verified. The repo does not record what they say of the fellowships after 2010.
livingEvidence.grade: none (no dated item after 2010 is in the repo)

otherLinksToLivingEntries.otherName: East African Christianity & the Uganda Martyrs
The Anglican Communion in the Twentieth Century
The Anglican Communion in the Twentieth Century

statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window ends in 1977, the martyrdom of Archbishop Janani Luwum, rather than a soft decade round-off; the fellowships lived on inside East African Anglicanism after it.
relationsSummary: African-led within (and often against) mission Anglicanism; martyrs include Janani Luwum. The revival began in Rwanda. The entry on the Catholic Church in Africa tells of the churches and Rwanda's genocide of 1994.
why: The revival began around 1930 at the mission station at Gahini in Rwanda, when African and missionary Christians started confessing sin to each other out loud, in public. Those who joined were called balokole, "the saved ones," and they carried the movement through Rwanda, Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania on testimony, shared meetings, and a hymn, "Tukutendereza Yesu," sung wherever they gathered. Archbishop Janani Luwum, killed in 1977, became its best-known martyr.
legacy: The revival came as a wave, and by the 1970s the wave had passed. The fellowships had not. They lived on inside the Anglican churches of East Africa. They kept their meetings, their practice of confession and their hymn. The revival gave those churches a generation of African leaders. They were formed outside the control of missions. It also left a large body of testimony, and historians were slow to read it. Janani Luwum is honored among the twentieth-century martyrs on the west front of Westminster Abbey, unveiled in 1998.

name: African-Initiated Churches (Harrist; Aladura; Zionist/ZCC; Kimbanguist)

(2019): counter for AIC adherence; verified. The Ecumenical Movement & the World Council of Churches
The Anglican Communion in the Twentieth Century
African Diaspora & Reverse-Mission Churches in Europe

statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1), assessed body by body, as a family this varied must be. Its start reaches back to the 1880s, on the family's own historiography. The Kimbanguist church's dated documentary arc runs from its 2005 doctrine to the 2008 Nkamba reversal. It is disclosed as a real divergence, not harmonized away. The Harrist and Aladura mainstreams read as clearly outgrowing their founders; the Kimbanguist question stays open, and so does the ZCC's, which published little by its own choice.
relationsSummary: Many of these churches began when African Christians left the mission churches. Scholars still debate how much they owed to Pentecostal teaching. African founders led them, and they were fully the work of neither.
why: William Wadé Harris walked through the Ivory Coast and the Gold Coast between 1913 and 1915, preaching and baptizing, and the churches that trace to him took his name. Others rose on their own ground: Simon Kimbangu's ministry in Congo began in March 1921 and ended within months in a colonial court, while Engenas Lekganyane founded the Zion Christian Church in South Africa in 1924. Each carried its founder's legacy forward differently, from Nigeria's Aladura congregations to the ZCC's annual pilgrimage at Moria.
legacy: By 2010 these were established churches, several of them very large. The Zion Christian Church's pilgrimage to Moria was central to its life, and the Kimbanguist church was the first African-initiated church admitted to the World Council of Churches, in 1969. Their congregations traveled with African migration and were planted across Europe, a chapter this map tells in a separate entry. They also changed the scholarship: Bengt Sundkler's Bantu Prophets in South Africa (1948) and J. D. Y. Peel's Aladura (1968) made these churches a standard subject rather than a footnote to mission history.

otherLinksToLivingEntries.otherName: The Missionary Movement's Native Churches (Serampore India; Sierra Leone & the Niger; Pacific Islands; China Coast & CIM)

statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1), with safety binding every line of it. Assessed only on published texts, whether its sources reach beyond a single voice stays genuinely open. The 2009 Christian Research Institute reassessment is its dated counter-note, and the November 1998 house-church Confession of Faith is its own-voice anchor. No non-public person or community is identified anywhere in it, and where a fuller answer would need unsafe specificity, the entry says so and leaves the question open.
relationsSummary: The clearest twentieth-century echo of the house churches of Christianity's first two centuries, when congregations met quietly under pressure with no institutional standing.
why: From the 1910s Chinese Christians began founding churches of their own, free of the foreign missions. Wei Enbo's True Jesus Church dates from 1917, Watchman Nee's Little Flock from 1922, and the Jesus Family from 1927. Their leaders wrote a great deal and paid for it. Nee was imprisoned from 1952 to 1972, and Wang Mingdao from 1955 to 1980. In the decades that followed, much of the church went on meeting in homes. It was led by people with no institutional standing. That pattern, congregations meeting quietly under pressure, echoes the house churches of Christianity's first two centuries.
legacy: By 2010 it was a very large church by any count, though how large was genuinely contested. A Pew study published later, in 2011, estimated about 67 million Christians in China. Official Three-Self figures and the movements' own claims fell elsewhere, and the spread between them is itself worth knowing. The founder corpora were read far outside China. The longest inheritance may be the shape rather than the size: congregations meeting in homes, led by people with no institutional standing, carrying on through decades in which the alternative was prison. That pattern is the map's strongest modern echo of the house-churches of the first two centuries.

statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). Its tradition is closed, so its status is settled history. Barmen's drafting is cross-referenced to the mainline-century entry rather than carried twice.
relationsSummary: Lutheran/Reformed lines under catastrophe
why: When the Nazi state moved to take over the German Protestant churches in 1933, pastors organized in resistance, and a synod at Barmen in May 1934 declared that the church has one Word to obey, Jesus Christ, and no other. Dietrich Bonhoeffer ran an illegal seminary at Finkenwalde until it was shut down in 1937, writing Discipleship and Life Together out of that community before his own imprisonment. The movement's own historians are honest that its fight was mostly about the church's own freedom, and that its near-silence about what was happening to Jews is part of that story too.
legacy: The Confessing Church ended with the war, and this map treats it as a closed story rather than a living one. What it left is out of all proportion to its twelve years. The Barmen Declaration was taken up well beyond Germany. The Book of Confessions of the Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.), for one, includes it. It is cited whenever a church has to say what it will not concede to a state. Bonhoeffer's Letters and Papers from Prison, edited by Bethge and published in 1951, came to be read far outside the church struggle it came from. And the Stuttgart Declaration of Guilt set a pattern that other churches used in the decades that followed. It showed a church saying plainly what it had failed to do.

livingEvidence.evidence: L'Arche International, Summary Report of the independent inquiry (22 Feb 2020): own voice; [S]; Commission d'etude independante, Emprise et abus, report to L'Arche International (30 Jan 2023): independent commission, commissioned and published by the movement; [S]; L'Arche International, statement on Thomas Philippe (2016): own voice; [S]; Catholic Worker, Focolare, Charismatic Renewal: no dated source after 2010.
livingEvidence.grade: CR (Contemporary-Reported); newest dated item 2023, none verified

statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), assessed as four distinct movements rather than one tradition. All four appear, on the documented record, to have institutionalized beyond their founders. The L'Arche founder-abuse record rests on later documents the movement itself published. These are its commissioned inquiry of 2020 and the independent Study Commission report of 2023.
relationsSummary: Lay Catholics started four movements in the twentieth century. The Catholic Worker came first, in 1933, then Focolare in 1943. Next came L'Arche in 1964 and the Charismatic Renewal in 1967. Each one began on its own.
why: Four movements, each begun by lay Catholics and all still active in 2010: Dorothy Day and Peter Maurin's Catholic Worker in 1933, with its newspaper and houses of hospitality; Chiara Lubich's Focolare in 1943; the Charismatic Renewal that began on a retreat weekend at Duquesne University in 1967; and Jean Vanier's L'Arche in 1964, where people with and without intellectual disabilities share a household. L'Arche's story includes the abuse committed by Vanier himself across decades of his leadership. Later inquiries, which the movement commissioned and published in 2020 and 2023, documented it.
legacy: All four were still going in 2010. Catholic Worker houses of hospitality still operated and the paper still appeared. Focolare had become an international movement with statutes approved by Rome. The Charismatic Renewal reshaped ordinary parish life across the Catholic world within a generation.

otherLinksToLivingEntries.otherName: Latin American Catholicism in the Twentieth Century

statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window closes in the 1990s, the base-community contraction of that decade, marking an episode's end within a tradition that lived on.
relationsSummary: Pentecostal churches grew fast among the same poor communities in Latin America at the same time as the base communities, a pairing worth noting side by side. The base communities themselves contracted in the 1990s. But the pastoral practice they pioneered, and the communities' own heirs, continued inside Latin American church life. The bishops' meetings at Medellín in 1968 and Puebla in 1979 are told in the entry on Latin American Catholicism, the parent of this one.
why: From the 1960s, poor Catholics across Latin America began meeting in small groups to read the Bible against their own week, a practice the bishops backed at Medellín in 1968. At Solentiname in Nicaragua, Ernesto Cardenal published four volumes of what his peasant neighbors actually said about the Sunday gospel, one of the few places anywhere poor people's theology survives in their own words. Many of these communities' people were killed for it, among them Archbishop Óscar Romero, shot at the altar in March 1980.
legacy: The base communities contracted in the 1990s, and the movement was no longer what it had been. But the tradition lived on. Its pastoral practice, its small reading groups and the communities' own heirs continued inside Latin American church life. The Solentiname volumes went into several languages. Pentecostal churches grew fast among exactly the same poor at exactly the same time, and any account of one that leaves out the other is not describing what happened.

statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window ends in 1970, the OCA's autocephaly and the Paris generation's institutional handoff to the American Orthodoxy entry. One genealogy nuance: the Bulgakov/Berdyaev renaissance stands beside the Optina thread rather than simply continuing it.
relationsSummary: The Russian Revolution scattered a generation of Orthodox monks, thinkers and parishioners across Europe, many settling in Paris. Its roots run through more than one strand of Russian religious life — the Optina monastic tradition and the religious-philosophical renaissance associated with Sergei Bulgakov and Nikolai Berdyaev both feed into it. Much of English-speaking Orthodoxy in the twentieth century descended from this Paris generation. The church the émigrés left behind in Russia has its own entry, the Russian Orthodox Church.
why: The Russian revolution scattered a generation of Orthodox monks, thinkers and parishioners across Europe, and many landed in Paris, where the St Sergius Institute opened in 1925. Mother Maria Skobtsova ran a hostel there, sheltered Jews under the German occupation, and died at Ravensbrück on 31 March 1945. Vladimir Lossky's Mystical Theology of the Eastern Church, written in French and published in 1944, put Orthodox theology in front of Western readers for the first time.
legacy: The Paris generation's own episode closed around 1970, with the handoff its institutions had been building toward: the Orthodox Church in America received autocephaly in 1970, and St Vladimir's Seminary in New York became the school this tradition had built in a second country. Much of English-speaking Orthodoxy is descended from here. Skobtsova was canonized in 2004. Schmemann's For the Life of the World was put into students' hands in every tradition. Lossky became the book people were given when they asked what Orthodox theology actually says.

The study is of Habib Girgis, who died in 1951, so it does not describe the present by itself. The 21 Libya martyrs entered in the church's synaxarium (2015): own voice; [S]; Girgis canonized (2013): own voice; [S]; Mosebach, The 21 (ET 2019): literary journalism; [S].
livingEvidence.grade: CR (Contemporary-Reported); newest dated item 2019, newest verified 2017

statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window starts in the 1940s. The earlier Habib Girgis material - his teaching from the 1890s and the 1918 General Sunday School Committee - sits before this window and is disclosed rather than folded in. Whether the 1918 date itself is verified is unsettled.
relationsSummary: The same Coptic Orthodox Church carried both renewals. In 1969 monks went back to the Monastery of St Macarius in the desert, a house founded in the fourth century.
why: Habib Girgis built a church-wide Sunday-school movement from the 1890s that trained generations of teachers and, later, bishops, while from mid-century the Egyptian desert monasteries, long emptying, filled again under Patriarch Kyrillos VI.
legacy: By 2010 it was a living church whose lane on this map ran back, unbroken, to the desert fathers themselves. The Sunday schools had become the church's teaching system and the route by which much of its clergy was formed. The monasteries had filled again. Matthew the Poor's books found readers in traditions with no connection to Egypt at all. This church had always kept its martyrs in its liturgy: not remembered in the abstract, but named.

otherLinksToLivingEntries.otherName: African Diaspora & Reverse-Mission Churches in Europe

statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). Its prosperity-gospel line rests on dated texts. Scale claims about this family are checked against an independent count wherever one exists, or marked plainly as the movement's own self-report where none does.
relationsSummary: It grew from two roots: the revival that began at Azusa Street, and Africa's own prayer churches. Scholars disagree on how much the first gave. It was the growing edge of the century. El Shaddai, a Catholic movement in the Philippines, belongs to the story of Philippine Catholicism.
why: By the second half of the century, the weight of Pentecostal Christianity had shifted south, carried by churches founded in the Global South by people from it: the Redeemed Christian Church of God in Nigeria in 1952, Yoido Full Gospel Church in Seoul in 1958, the Igreja Universal in Brazil in 1977. These churches argued fiercely among themselves over prosperity teaching. The argument is on the public record in their own sermons. It is also in the published critiques of the Lausanne movement and of African evangelical theologians who rejected it.
legacy: In 2010 this was the map's growing edge, not a finished story. Counts of it need care. The very large totals combine denominational self-counts with surveys that define who is being counted in different ways. The spread between them tells you as much as the totals do. What is not in doubt is the direction of travel. By 2010 Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity had become largely a Global South matter. This map carries a separate entry for the congregations these churches planted back in Europe. The scholarship followed. Anderson, Martin, Kalu and others made this the central subject of world Christianity rather than its margin.

otherLinksToLivingEntries.otherName: Russian Evangelicals — Stundists to the Baptist Union

statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window ends in 1991, a documented terminus. The dissolution of the USSR ended the persecution regime that defines this row; its member movements lived on beyond it.
relationsSummary: Its Baptist wing grew out of the Russian evangelical churches of the century before. Like China's house churches in the same years, its churches would not register on the state's terms. No direct tie between the two has been shown.
why: In the Soviet Union, a group of Baptist ministers broke in 1961 with the state-registered union and ran their own underground press; their Council of Prisoners' Relatives began issuing bulletins in 1964 that listed arrests and confiscations by name, week by week. In Romania, the Lord's Army, founded by the priest Iosif Trifa in 1923, continued under Communist rule, and its hymn-writer Traian Dorz left prison memoirs behind. When the Soviet archives opened after 1991, the persecutors' own files could finally be read alongside the persecuted's.
legacy: The persecution these movements faced ended with the fall of Communism across the Eastern bloc, and with the end of the Soviet Union in 1991. The movements themselves lived on. Their samizdat came to be seen as some of the best records anywhere of what religious persecution looks like from below. These were not lives of martyrs written long after. They were bulletins written that week, listing who had been taken and from where. The Keston archive kept much of it. In China, unregistered churches refused the state's terms over the same decades. The two stories run side by side, but no direct tie between them has been shown.

name: Messianic Judaism

livingEvidence.basis: A church body, or a set of them, with no recorded end; the gap is in the citation. CD if the Pew 2013 figures are verified. Newest evidence is thirteen years old.
livingEvidence.evidence: Pew US Jewish survey (2013), touching Messianic self-identification: independent survey; figures [S]; Rudolph & Willitts, Introduction to Messianic Judaism (2013): movement scholars; verified.
livingEvidence.grade: CR (Contemporary-Reported); newest dated item 2013, newest verified 2013

statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), with its double-direction sensitivity kept in view throughout. Its confessional note on the doctrinal floor carries its own dates, and its boundary with the largely gentile Torah-observance current is drawn, not blurred. That current is a separate entry, and the two movements' own publications draw the line between them.
relationsSummary: Messianic Judaism raises a question as old as the church: can a person be fully Jewish and follow Jesus? The first Jewish believers argued over it. In the book of Acts, the believers in Jerusalem were "all zealous of the law". They heard that Paul taught Jews "to forsake Moses". This movement brought the question back in living form.
why: From the 1960s and 1970s, Jewish believers in Jesus began forming congregations that kept Sabbath, festivals and Hebrew liturgy rather than joining gentile churches. The Hebrew Christian Alliance of America, founded in 1915, renamed itself the Messianic Jewish Alliance in 1975, a change of name that was also a change of self-understanding. David Stern's Complete Jewish Bible, published in 1998, and the Union of Messianic Jewish Congregations' 2005 statement "Defining Messianic Judaism" are among the clearest attempts to say what the movement actually is.
legacy: By 2010 it was a living movement, with congregations in Israel and North America. For its size, it had written a great deal about what it is. Its Bible translation and its prayers for worship were used well beyond it. On this map, the question it kept open matters more than what it built. Can a person be fully Jewish and follow Jesus? The first Jewish believers argued over that, and this movement put it back in living form. Counting it was hard. The congregations' own figures and outside counts differed, and nothing independent settled it.

livingEvidence.grade: CR (Contemporary-Reported); newest dated item 2023, none verified

statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). This is the clearest documented case in this era. Brother Roger was murdered on 16 August 2005, and the community continued under Brother Alois - a completed founder-to-successor transition.
relationsSummary: Two communities of shared life, work and prayer, founded in the 1930s and 1940s. The Iona Community rebuilt the abbey on Columba's own island. No source shows what either took from the older monastic houses.
why: George MacLeod founded the Iona Community in 1938 and set it to rebuilding the abbey on Columba's own island, a project that took until 1965. Roger Schutz began the community at Taizé in France two years later, in 1940, and from the 1970s young people started arriving by the thousands, for meetings held every year from 1978. When Brother Roger was murdered in 2005, the community simply continued under Brother Alois.
legacy: Both communities were still going in 2010, and both took visitors. Taizé's European meetings were held every year from 1978. Iona's Wild Goose material, much of it by John Bell, found its way into hymnals across the English-speaking world. Their passage through the death of a founder is itself part of what they left. Taizé carried on under Brother Alois, so the community outlived the man who began it.

otherLinksToLivingEntries.otherName: The Way International; Unification Church; La Luz del Mundo

statusDescription: Assessed body by body, as its own record calls for. Its window runs to 2010, the era's end, not 1993, which rested on no real event. There is no single founder to test here, so its status rests on the doctrinal floor alone.
relationsSummary: Oneness Pentecostalism grew out of the wider Pentecostal movement that came after the Azusa Street revival. Two other churches share those roots. One is the True Jesus Church, founded in Beijing in 1917. The other is La Luz del Mundo in Mexico. Its founder came to faith among Oneness believers there in the 1920s.
why: In April 1913, at the Arroyo Seco camp meeting, R. E. McAlister preached that the baptisms recorded in Acts were performed in the name of Jesus alone, and the following year Frank Ewart and Glenn Cook baptized each other on that basis. When the Assemblies of God adopted an explicitly trinitarian statement of faith in 1916, the ministers who could not sign it left and formed their own bodies, among them the interracial Pentecostal Assemblies of the World, long led by G. T. Haywood. Baptism in the name of Jesus alone was what a visitor to these churches noticed first.
legacy: By 2010 these were living churches with congregations worldwide. Their mark, baptism in the name of Jesus, was what a visitor noticed first. Their size was hard to fix. The figures in use were the bodies' own, with no outside count to check them. Two other churches share these roots. The True Jesus Church was founded in Beijing in 1917. The founder of La Luz del Mundo in Mexico came to faith among Oneness believers.

statusDescription: A composite entry covering three distinct bodies. Each is assessed on its own dated texts, not treated as one group. Its window starts in 1926, the founding of the earliest body it covers.
relationsSummary: Three separately founded bodies share this entry. They did not share a creed, and each body's own texts carry its own finding. Scholars trace La Luz del Mundo to the Oneness Pentecostal movement. The church itself does not call itself Pentecostal. Iglesia ni Cristo has its own entry.
why: Three separately founded movements share this entry. The Way International grew out of Victor Paul Wierwille's radio ministry in the 1940s. Sun Myung Moon founded the Unification Church in Seoul in 1954. La Luz del Mundo was founded in Guadalajara in 1926, and from 1964 a second apostle led it in succession from its founder. Each has its own scripture, founder claim and history, told here on its own terms.
legacy: All three were still active in 2010. La Luz del Mundo had one change of leader, in 1964. The Way had two after its founder. The Unification Church was still led by its founder. Court records were part of these bodies' public record too. The Way's leadership changes ran alongside litigation, and in 1982 a federal jury convicted Sun Myung Moon of filing false tax returns.

otherLinksToLivingEntries.otherName: The Seventh-day Adventist Church in the 20th Century

statusDescription: Kept at this family's edge for the map's own honesty. Its window is 1929-1993, a documented terminus; remnant groups that outlasted 1993 are disclosed only in those terms - no later community and no non-public person is identified.
relationsSummary: In 1929 Victor Houteff began to spread a reform message inside Adventism, and his church rejected it. His followers settled at Mount Carmel outside Waco in 1935. Leadership passed to the Branch group under Ben and Lois Roden in 1955, then to David Koresh in the 1980s. A federal siege from 28 February to 19 April 1993 ended in a fire that killed 76 people. Much of what is known about how the siege ended comes from the government side. It comes from hearings in Congress and from the Danforth Report. The community itself did not survive to tell its own story.
why: In 1929 Victor Houteff began to spread a reform message inside Adventism, and he published it as The Shepherd's Rod. His followers settled at Mount Carmel outside Waco in 1935. Leadership passed to Ben and Lois Roden's Branch group in 1955 and then to David Koresh in the 1980s. On 28 February 1993 a federal raid began a siege. It ended on 19 April in a fire that killed 76 people. Koresh's own account of the seven seals was left unfinished.
legacy: The community at Mount Carmel was destroyed in 1993, and the movement ended there. Small remnant groups outlasted 1993, but none of their members is named or described here. The siege provoked a scholarship of its own: Tabor and Gallagher's Why Waco? (1995) and Kenneth Newport's study of 2006. It asked what the group actually believed, a question the congressional hearings had largely not asked. It also changed how researchers and law-enforcement agencies approached religious groups under siege.

statusDescription: This is a broad label, not one movement, so no single finding is made on it. Its illustrations carry their own dates, and its reasoning rests on published statements rather than communities in the aggregate. The mainline-century entry is its parent, named in both directions.
relationsSummary: Progressive Christianity covers mainline progressive congregations, post-evangelical networks, and much in between, with the emerging church of the 1990s and 2000s as its most documented expression. It descends from the mainline century of liberal Protestantism and neo-orthodoxy, which hands off to it around 1990.
why: Progressive Christianity is a label, not one movement: it covers old mainline parishes with a century of history behind them, congregations founded in the 2000s, and simply readers of particular books, with no single founder or confession linking them all. The Center for Progressive Christianity, founded in 1994, published its own set of guiding points and revised them, and each version is its own dated statement.
legacy: In 2010 it was a current still in motion, and what it would leave behind was not yet settled. Two things can be said of it by then. It has a history that reaches further back than the word does: the mainline century of liberal Protestantism and neo-orthodoxy is its parent, and hands off to it around 1990. And it had a documented movement expression in the emerging church of the 1990s and 2000s. That is where most of the writing and conference records are. The label itself did something a movement could not: it gave very different congregations a word they could find each other by.

statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), and the Syriac lane's resumption. It also names the Assyrian wing's own arc, which would otherwise vanish inside a Syriac-Orthodox-shaped row.
relationsSummary: This is the modern continuation of the ancient Syriac Christian tradition, whose recorded history had gone quiet after about 1300 — a silence Syriac communities experienced as erasure, named honestly here rather than smoothed over. It covers the Assyrian, Church of the East wing as well as the Syriac Orthodox wing, including the assassination of Mar Shimun XXIII in 1975, a split within the Church of the East in 1968, and the 1994 Common Christological Declaration with Rome.
why: In 1915, Syriac Christians across eastern Anatolia were massacred and driven from their homes in what survivors called the Sayfo, the sword; Joseph Naayem, a survivor and priest, published his account, Shall This Nation Die?, within six years. What followed was a century of relocation: the Syriac Orthodox patriarchate moved to Homs in 1933 and then Damascus in 1959, while exiled communities of the Church of the East regathered as far away as Chicago. The Assyrian wing of this history kept writing its own hard chapters, including the assassination of Mar Shimun XXIII in 1975 and a Common Christological Declaration with Rome in 1994.
legacy: In 2010 the lane was alive, and its communities lived mostly somewhere other than where they started. By then the Sayfo had its standard scholarly study, David Gaunt's of 2006, built on archives and the survivors' oral histories. The edited collection Let Them Not Return followed later, in 2017. On this map the entry does one more thing: it carries the oldest lane on the whole atlas honestly to 2010, after a silence from around 1300 that Syriac Christians experienced, understandably, as erasure. The silence is named rather than smoothed over, and this is where the lane resumes.

statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window starts in 1900, the seamless continuation of the Ethiopian re-foundation century before it.
relationsSummary: The Tawahedo church lived on through empire, war and the Derg's attacks on it. Beside it grew the P'ent'ay, a fast-growing movement of evangelicals. It carries on the church of Tewodros and Menelik.
why: Italian occupying forces massacred the monks of Debre Libanos in 1937, and decades later Ethiopia's Communist Derg deposed the country's patriarch, Tewophilos, in 1976 and killed him in 1979 -- a history the Tawahedo church took into its own liturgical memory. Alongside it, a Protestant evangelical movement called the P'ent'ay grew fastest precisely while it was forced underground under the Derg. Eritrea's church, autocephalous since 1993, faced its own severe pressure: in 2006 Patriarch Antonios was deposed and placed under house arrest.
legacy: In 2010 both churches were living. The Tawahedo was one of the largest ancient churches anywhere. Its own canon, calendar, liturgical language and fasting discipline were intact after a century that took the state away twice. By then the evangelical movement that grew beside it was a large minority in its own right. The relationship between the two was unresolved. The Derg-era martyrology became part of the church's own liturgical memory. Ethiopia's patriarchal disputes ran on after 1991 and were still unresolved in 2010; Eritrea's church was under severe pressure.

statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window ends in 1989, a documented terminus: the church's legalization.
relationsSummary: The world's largest banned church - clandestine ordinations, bishops in the Gulag, emergence intact in 1989; a continuation of the Union of Brest. The Romanian Greek Catholic Church, dissolved in 1948, has its own entry.
why: In March 1946, a synod at Lviv dissolved the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church into the Russian Orthodox Church -- with every one of its own bishops already under arrest and none present to agree to it. For the next forty-three years priests were ordained in secret and liturgies held in apartments and forests, while Metropolitan Josyf Slipyj spent from 1945 to 1963 in the camps. When the church was finally legalized in 1989, it came back with its hierarchy, parishes and people still intact.
legacy: Legalization in 1989 ended the underground, and by 2010 the church that emerged was the largest of the Eastern Catholic churches. Its survival became a standing counter-example to the assumption that a church without buildings, seminaries, publishing or legal existence will simply fade — it did none of those things for four decades and came back whole. The record it left is unusual in having both halves: the confessors' own letters and testimony, and the archives of the agencies that hunted them, which could be read side by side once the archives opened after 1991.

statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window ends in 1991, a documented terminus. relationsSummary: The century's largest persecution of Christians - Solovki, Butovo, the catacomb communities, thousands of canonized new martyrs; the Optina tradition carried through catastrophe. The church's story as an institution has its own entry, the Russian Orthodox Church. That entry runs from the Council of 1917 to the Act of Canonical Communion of 2007.
why: Thousands of clergy, monastics and laypeople were shot at the Butovo firing range outside Moscow in 1937 and 1938 alone, while the ancient Solovki monastery became a prison camp. When Metropolitan Sergius declared loyalty to the Soviet state in 1927, the church split, and those who refused to commemorate him in the liturgy followed bishops like Joseph of Petrograd into hidden catacomb communities instead. In August 2000, the Moscow patriarchate canonized these new martyrs and confessors by the thousands.
legacy: The persecution ended with the Soviet Union in 1991, and the church that survived it was very much alive in 2010. Its story as an institution has its own entry, the Russian Orthodox Church. What this century left is a martyrology of a scale the church had to build new instruments to hold — the new-martyrs database built after the archives opened, the Butovo lists, oral-history projects. It also left an argument the church was still having with itself in 2010, about the 1927 Declaration and what compliance cost, which the surviving documents from both sides keep open.

statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) — the council's own texts carry it directly, the clearest case on this map. Its traditionalist tension rests on dated documents.
relationsSummary: This is the Second Vatican Council as it was lived in parishes: Mass in the vernacular, lay ministries, and in 1972 the restoration of the Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults, reviving a catechumenate pattern from Christianity's first centuries. The council's own documents — Sacrosanctum Concilium (1963), Lumen Gentium (1964), and Gaudium et Spes (1965) — carry these changes. The tension with traditionalists who preferred the older Latin rite is documented in the church's own successive rulings: Ecclesia Dei (1988) and Summorum Pontificum (2007). After the council, Asia's bishops formed a federation of their own. In 1970, 180 Catholic bishops of Asia met in Manila, and Paul VI was present for its last part. The Federation of Asian Bishops' Conferences, the FABC, dates its birth to that meeting. It traces its roots to the council, where many Asian bishops first came to know one another.
why: The Second Vatican Council's liturgy constitution, promulgated on 4 December 1963, changed what most Catholics actually experienced on a Sunday: Mass in their own language, readers and ministers drawn from the pews, parish councils. In 1972 the church restored the Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults, bringing back a first-century pattern of preparing converts that had lain dormant for fifteen centuries. The disagreement over the older Latin rite had not settled by 2010. The church kept restating its own position in dated documents: Ecclesia Dei in 1988, Summorum Pontificum in 2007.
legacy: By 2010 most of the world's Catholics had worshipped this way for more than forty years. By then the restored catechumenate was the normal way for adults to join the Catholic Church. Mass in people's own language and lay ministries had become so much a part of life that they no longer felt new. In 2010 the argument over the older rite was still open. The church's own dated rulings record it, from Ecclesia Dei in 1988 to Summorum Pontificum in 2007.

statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1), and it carries the era's best-documented self-description ladder — a three-dated confession series from Lausanne 1974 through Manila 1989 to Cape Town 2010. Its region coding reads as global, matching its own record; it stands as the counter-pole to the conciliar ecumenical movement, in both directions.
relationsSummary: At the 1974 Congress, Global South voices — chiefly the Latin Americans René Padilla and Samuel Escobar — argued for holding evangelism and social responsibility together, bending the whole movement toward what became known as integral mission. It worked as a network rather than a denomination, restating itself through a series of dated documents: the Lausanne Covenant (1974), the Manila Manifesto (1989) and the Cape Town Commitment (2010). It stands as a counter-pole to the conciliar ecumenical movement centered on Geneva — two different twentieth-century answers to how separated churches should act together. At the 1974 Congress, Ralph and Roberta Winter prepared a paper on the peoples that existing missions did not reach. In 1997 the Southern Baptist International Mission Board took up an approach called the Church Planting Movement. David Garrison set it out in a book in 2004. Evangelical relief agencies worked on the same ground, and some were older than the congress. Tearfund grew out of the Evangelical Alliance in 1968. Brian Stanley's history names this evangelical age after Billy Graham and John Stott. Graham's evangelistic association was incorporated in 1950. In 1971 the Kenyan theologian John Gatu called for a moratorium on missionaries. At Lausanne in 1974 most leaders appeared to reject a broad moratorium. Still, the Lausanne Covenant allowed that fewer foreign missionaries might sometimes help a national church grow in self-reliance. The Christian Right, a political movement that American ministers began with the Moral Majority in 1979, has a separate entry.
why: At the Lausanne Congress in July 1974, the Latin American theologians René Padilla and Samuel Escobar argued that evangelism and social responsibility could not be separated, and they won enough of the room to bend the whole movement in that direction -- which is why "integral mission" became a Lausanne word. What came out of the congress was not a denomination but a network built around a document, the Lausanne Covenant, and the movement restated itself twice more, in the Manila Manifesto of 1989 and the Cape Town Commitment of 2010.
legacy: In 2010 it was a living network rather than a church, and that was the point. It convened, published and connected, and the churches doing the work belonged to other bodies entirely. Its 1974 covenant became the network's shared statement. By 2010 'integral mission' (evangelism and social action held together) had become mainstream evangelical language. That was largely because of what the Global South delegates said in 1974. It stands as the counter-pole to the conciliar ecumenical movement centered on Geneva: two different answers, from the same century, to the question of how separated churches should act together.
