statusDescription: Tiered deferred on a smaller frame (Tier 3). It is assessed through named carrier bodies rather than as one current with a single confession. Where no single body speaks for the whole, that shape is stated plainly rather than smoothed over.
relationsSummary: Within a single lifetime, the direction of Christian mission reversed. By 2010 churches once planted in Africa by European missionaries were planting congregations back among Europeans. It continued a pattern as old as Christianity itself — faith traveling with people who have been scattered from their homes.
why: Within a single lifetime the mission map turned over: by 2010 churches that European missionaries had once planted in Africa were planting congregations back among Europeans. The Redeemed Christian Church of God, founded in Nigeria in 1952, opened Jesus House in London in 1994, the same year Sunday Adelaja founded the Embassy of the Blessed Kingdom of God for All Nations in Kyiv. Aladura and Kimbanguist congregations had already been meeting in European cities since the 1960s, the earliest layer of what came to be called reverse mission.
legacy: In 2010 this was a current in progress rather than a finished chapter, and it was not one confession. The churches involved came from several different African traditions and answered to their own bodies. Claims that one or another was the largest congregation in Britain or in Europe circulated widely and rested mostly on the churches' own counts. What is clear is that by 2010 the direction of Christian mission had reversed within living memory. By then European Christianity's growing edge was often African. It is also the map's newest instance of its oldest pattern: the faith traveling with people who have been scattered.

statusDescription: Its own framing question stays genuinely open: the office persisted by succession through the century, which points toward it outgrowing any one founder. The other bodies grouped with it are named only minimally, since each must be named before it can be assessed on its own.
relationsSummary: These movements grew out of Pacific mission Christianity, led by local people. Tahupōtiki Wiremu Rātana had a vision on 8 November 1918. His church, Te Haahi Rātana, was set up in 1925. A like pattern shows up elsewhere in the Pacific. The best-known case is Silas Eto's Christian Fellowship Church in the Solomon Islands. It began around 1960.
why: After a vision in 1918, Tahupōtiki Wiremu Rātana founded Te Haahi Rātana in Aotearoa New Zealand in 1925. The church calls him the mangai, the mouthpiece, and the title runs through its own creed and hymns. The movement became a political force as well as a religious one. It took a Treaty of Waitangi petition to London in 1924. By 1943 it held all four Māori seats in Parliament. Similar movements arose elsewhere in the Pacific. One is Silas Eto's Christian Fellowship Church in the Solomon Islands, which began around 1960.
legacy: In 2010 Te Haahi Rātana was a living church and still a force in New Zealand public life. The annual gathering at Rātana Pā was a fixture of the political calendar. Both sides still referred to the alliance made in 1936. The movement gave Māori Christianity an institutional form that was not a mission's, at a time when almost nothing else was on offer. The questions this map records about it — what the mangai's mediating role means, put to the church's own prayers rather than to its members — are held here as questions, in the terms the church's own texts set.

relationsSummary: This is the modern continuation of one of Christianity's oldest churches, tracing back to antiquity in the Caucasus, and it shares a history of suffering under Soviet rule with other churches from the region.
why: In 1915 the Armenian genocide left the church's homeland base destroyed, its clergy killed and its dioceses emptied, and what survived did so by moving — the Holy See of Cilicia relocated to Antelias, Lebanon, in 1930, while Etchmiadzin endured under Soviet rule. By 2010 its worldwide diaspora outnumbered the church in Armenia itself.
legacy: In 2010 the church was alive in Armenia and in a diaspora larger than the church at home. It was one of the oldest churches anywhere with an unbroken life. Its Mother See at Etchmiadzin dates its founding to the early fourth century. The Cold War split between Etchmiadzin and Antelias had eased by 2010. But it shaped the life of the diaspora for generations. And the record of this century has to be handled the way its own people handled it: as living memory, not distant history.

relationsSummary: It grew out of late evangelicalism as it met the postmodern turn. It overlapped with new monastic communities, which began in the same years. In 2004 more than sixty people in Durham, North Carolina, drafted the twelve marks of the new monasticism. The emerging church may also be the best-recorded part of the wider progressive Christian current. How far it fed that current has not been traced in detail.
why: Beginning in the late 1990s, younger evangelical leaders in North America, Britain and Australia used books, blogs and loose networks like Emergent Village to question a church they felt was answering questions nobody was asking. The conversation deliberately left confessional questions open rather than settling them, and its record was kept mostly on blogs and other fragile platforms.
legacy: In 2010 the conversation was still active, and Emergent Village was still its main network. The map closes it at 2010 because the era closes there, not because anything ended. Its questions may have fed the wider progressive current, though that path has not been traced in detail. It also left a problem of keeping its record. A movement that wrote its story almost entirely online kept its archive there too.

statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), assessed through its own dated mass-texts, as a culture this diffuse must be. Its 31-year overlap with the Brethren entry is disclosed rather than re-dated away - the honest shape of a culture that outlived the body that formed it. Its claim of millions of readers rests on those dated texts.
relationsSummary: This popular culture grew out of Plymouth Brethren teaching, carried forward through the Bible-institute tradition. It reached a mass audience mainly through print: the Scofield Reference Bible (1909, revised 1917), Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth (1970), and the sixteen Left Behind novels (1995–2007). Dallas Theological Seminary's doctrinal statement was its clearest institutional anchor.
why: Beginning with the Niagara Bible Conference's prophecy teaching in the 1870s, this way of reading scripture in distinct dispensations leading to a rapture spread less through preaching than through print: the Scofield Reference Bible of 1909 put the scheme in footnotes that readers met every time they opened the text. Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth in 1970 and the sixteen Left Behind novels published between 1995 and 2007 carried it to a mass audience far larger than any single denomination.
legacy: In 2010 the culture was alive and its texts were in print. It gave a large part of English-speaking Protestantism a default way of reading the Bible. It also gave a default sense of how history ends, carried more by study notes, charts and novels than by any pulpit. It had institutional anchors — Dallas Theological Seminary's doctrinal statement among them — but it never needed a denomination. It also produced its own opposition. The reading of the Bible as one story fulfilled in Jesus, carried elsewhere on this map, became its rival. In 2001 N. T. Wright, a leading writer of the story reading, wrote against the rapture. By 2010 the scholarship on it was substantial, from Sandeen (1970) and Weber (1979) to Boyer's When Time Shall Be No More (1992). Hummel's study came later, in 2023.

why: From 1975, when Willow Creek Community Church designed its Sunday service for people who don't go to church, a model built on small groups and contemporary worship spread from American suburbs worldwide, carried in part by songs written by Hillsong, founded in Australia in 1983, and by 2010 sung far beyond anyone's knowledge of where they came from. In 2007 Willow Creek's own REVEAL study turned that same rigor on itself, asking whether its programs were forming anyone spiritually at all.

Its worship music was sung in congregations that had no idea where it came from. By then the Hartford Institute's research studied it as a serious subject rather than a curiosity. Kate Bowler's Blessed (2013) later did the same. In 2021 Lester Ruth and Lim Swee Hong published a history of contemporary praise and worship.

statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). It is assessed on its own dated texts, from The Fundamentals (1910–15) to the naming of 1920.
relationsSummary: Fundamentalism grew out of the Niagara Bible Conference of the 1870s and the Princeton doctrine of biblical inerrancy set out in 1881, decades before it took its name in 1920. It defended traditional Christian doctrine against theological liberalism, as in J. Gresham Machen's Christianity and Liberalism (1923), and suffered public defeats at the Scopes trial in 1925 and in Princeton Seminary's reorganization in 1929. Much of its constituency later moved into the neo-evangelical movement through the National Association of Evangelicals in 1942, Fuller Seminary in 1947, and Billy Graham's break with separatism in 1957, while its independent Baptist and separatist churches continued on their own. The networks gave radio evangelists such as Paul Rader and Charles Fuller no free time, so they bought airtime instead. In 1944 evangelical broadcasters formed the National Religious Broadcasters, at the invitation of the National Association of Evangelicals. Billy Graham's Los Angeles campaign of 1949 ran for more than eight weeks instead of the three planned. The political mobilization that began with the Moral Majority in 1979 also traces back to this movement, one step beyond its own historical window. The Christian Right has its own entry.
why: The name arrived in 1920, when Curtis Lee Laws called for 'battle royal for the Fundamentals' in the Watchman-Examiner, but the movement was older: twelve volumes called The Fundamentals, financed by Lyman Stewart and given away in some three million copies between 1910 and 1915, defended the doctrine of scripture A. A. Hodge and B. B. Warfield had set out in 1881. Public defeats followed — the Scopes trial in 1925, Princeton Seminary's reorganization in 1929 — before much of its constituency moved into the neo-evangelical world through the National Association of Evangelicals in 1942 and Billy Graham's 1957 break with separatism, while its independent Baptist and separatist churches carried on.
legacy: The movement was alive in 2010; this window is not its whole life. It closes at a documented handoff rather than a death — the National Association of Evangelicals in 1942, Fuller Seminary in 1947, and Billy Graham's break with separatist fundamentalism in 1957 carried much of its constituency into the neo-evangelical world that this map picks up again at Lausanne. What stayed behind kept going: the independent Baptist and separatist congregations and their institutions were still there in 2010. The political mobilization that began with the Moral Majority in 1979 sits one step past this window. It has its own entry, the Christian Right. George Marsden's Fundamentalism and American Culture (1980) became the standard account.

statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: This was the social-reform wing of the same era, beginning with Washington Gladden in 1886, Rauschenbusch's pastorate in Hell's Kitchen from that same year, and Charles Sheldon's novel in 1896. Its core period ran from 1907, when Christianity and the Social Crisis appeared, to Rauschenbusch's death in 1918. The Federal Council of Churches' 1908 Social Creed anchors it to the mainline Protestant tradition that later absorbed its stream into its own social agencies. Reinhold Niebuhr's 1932 critique challenged the movement's optimism from within that same broader current.
why: In 1886 Washington Gladden published Applied Christianity the same year Walter Rauschenbusch took a pastorate on the edge of New York's Hell's Kitchen, an experience that turned his theology toward social reform; his Christianity and the Social Crisis (1907) went through thirteen printings in five years. Charles Sheldon's 1896 novel In His Steps put the same impulse into a question anyone could ask before acting — what would Jesus do — while the Federal Council of Churches adopted the movement's own Social Creed in 1908. Rauschenbusch's death in 1918 and the war's blow to reform-minded optimism effectively ended the movement, though its stream flowed on into the mainline denominations' own social agencies.
legacy: The movement itself ended. Rauschenbusch died in 1918, and the war took the confidence out of a theology that expected the kingdom to arrive through reform. Reinhold Niebuhr's Moral Man and Immoral Society (1932) later made the criticism stick. But the stream did not stop. It was absorbed into the mainline churches' own social agencies, and the mainline century that followed took up its cause. The Social Creed of 1908 stands behind the church social statements that came after it. And In His Steps left something odder and longer-lasting. The question 'what would Jesus do' was still being asked a hundred years after the novel that put it there.

statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: This tradition reaches back to Schleiermacher and the historical-critical scholarship of the nineteenth century, including the Briggs heresy trial of 1891–93 and Harnack's work around 1900, and took institutional shape with the Federal Council of Churches in 1908. The fundamentalist-modernist controversy — Fosdick's sermon in 1922, Machen's reply in 1923, and the Auburn Affirmation in 1924 — stands in tension with fundamentalism as its opposite pole. From within liberal theology, Barth's turn to neo-orthodoxy (1919/1922) was carried further by Niebuhr, Bultmann, and Tillich; Barth's line also runs into the Confessing Church and the Barmen Declaration. The National Council of Churches, formed in 1950, and the World Council of Churches are this tradition's institutional and conciliar homes. Membership peaked in the mid-1960s and then declined, and this current hands off around 1990 to the current called progressive Christianity.
why: Harry Emerson Fosdick's 1922 sermon 'Shall the Fundamentalists Win?' and J. Gresham Machen's reply the following year opened a rupture that the Auburn Affirmation, eventually signed by some 1,300 mainline clergy, answered from the liberal side. From inside that same Christian tradition, Karl Barth's Romans commentary opened a neo-orthodox turn that Reinhold Niebuhr, Rudolf Bultmann and Paul Tillich each carried further, while the seminaries that trained the denominations' clergy watched membership peak in the mid-1960s before its long decline began.
legacy: The mainline churches were alive in 2010. What closed around 1990 was this one century of theirs. Their numbers peaked in the mid-1960s and fell after that. From around 1990 the people who carried their questions often called their faith progressive. They left large bodies behind: the National Council of Churches from 1950, a home in the World Council of Churches, and many seminaries. Those seminaries trained the clergy and wrote much of the century's Bible scholarship. Barth's line ran into the Confessing Church, whose Barmen Declaration he drafted. And the argument with fundamentalism, fought out in dated texts on both sides, was never settled.

relationsSummary: The HKBP, the Batak church, became fully independent in 1930. Between 1965 and 1966, in the wake of mass political violence and a new state requirement that every citizen declare a religion, church membership grew rapidly across the archipelago. A revival swept through Timor from 1965 to 1971 in the same period. In the decades that followed, Indonesian church life ran under the state ideology of Pancasila, with periodic episodes of persecution. Indonesia's Catholics are part of this story too. Karel Steenbrink called the years 1903 to 1942 "the spectacular growth of a self-confident minority". Jan Aritonang and Steenbrink's history of 2008 tells the Catholic and Protestant churches together.
why: The Batak church, the HKBP, became the first self-governing church in the Dutch East Indies in 1930. Between 1965 and 1971 a revival swept through Timor — recounted in Mel Tari's widely read but disputed Like a Mighty Wind (1971) and evaluated more carefully on the ground by George Peters in 1973 — in the same years that a state requirement to declare a religion, following the violence of 1965-66, drove rapid church growth across the archipelago.
legacy: In 2010 these were living churches, and large ones. Christians were a minority in the country, and their place was at times contested. The HKBP's independence in 1930 is an early marker of a long shift, from mission to self-governing church. The Timor revival left a widely read account in Mel Tari's book. Tari and Peters together are a rare case. A movement's own account and its critical evaluation survive side by side.

relationsSummary: The Mizo revivals that began in 1906 transformed the northeastern hills, helping make Mizoram and Nagaland among the most Christian regions on earth. In Kerala, the Mar Thoma Church — which separated as a reform wing from the wider Malankara St Thomas Christian community in 1889 — grew through the same century and spread with the Malayali diaspora.
why: Revival waves that ran through the Mizo hills from 1906 onward produced lengkhawm zai, hymns composed in the local language and manner of singing that became the churches' ordinary worship, and helped make Mizoram and Nagaland among the most heavily Christian regions on earth. legacy: Both were living churches in 2010. Their hymnody is one of the clearest cases anywhere of a Christian tradition composing in its own musical language rather than translating someone else's. relationsSummary: Alongside the Armenian church, this is one of the Caucasus region's modern anchors. Georgia's bishops unilaterally restored the church's autocephaly on 25 March 1917, reversing Russia's 1811 abolition of it. Ambrosi's 1922 protest memorandum and trial, and the Soviet decades that followed, tested the restored church before Moscow recognized it in 1943 and Constantinople in 1990. In the years after the Soviet Union's end, the church took a strong role in Georgia's national life.
why: Georgia's church had been autocephalous since antiquity until Russia abolished that status in 1811; in March 1917, without waiting for anyone's permission, an assembly of Georgian bishops, clergy and laypeople declared it restored, and a council that September elected Kyrion II as Catholicos-Patriarch, who was dead within a year under circumstances the record leaves unresolved. Recognition came slowly from two directions — Moscow acknowledged the restoration in 1943, Constantinople only in 1990 — after decades of Soviet rule that also saw Ambrosi tried in 1922 for a protest memorandum.
legacy: By 2010 it was a living national church, with an unusually strong place in its country's public life. Its restored autocephaly, declared unilaterally in 1917, was recognized by Moscow in 1943 and by Constantinople in 1990, after which no one contested it. On this map the entry answers a question left open at the previous era's close: whether the Caucasus lane resumes at all after 1811. It does, here. English-language scholarship on the modern Georgian church was thin, and this map names that thinness rather than papering over it.

relationsSummary: This is the a cappella wing of the movement, first distinguished from the Disciples of Christ in the 1906 United States religious census. Over the twentieth century it grew through colleges and world missions, and divided again at mid-century over whether congregations could support institutions in common, producing a non-institutional stream that lasted.

Its a cappella singing was the thing a visitor noticed first, and it remained the practice. Its refusal of denominational machinery held remarkably well: in 2010 there was still no headquarters to write to. Its mid-century division over institutional cooperation left a lasting non-institutional stream inside it.

relationsSummary: This is the Disciples of Christ wing that emerged from the 1906 division, later reorganizing itself into a denomination through the 1968 Restructure known as 'The Design.' why: After the 1906 division, the Disciples of Christ kept their instruments and their national organization, becoming founding members of the Federal Council of Churches in 1908 and the World Council of Churches in 1948 before adopting a 1968 plan called 'The Design' that turned a movement of congregations into a denomination. That step came after decades of quiet separation: congregations that became the independent Christian Churches had been meeting apart at the North American Christian Convention since 1927 and were listed separately in the yearbooks by 1971 — one plea for Christian unity having produced three distinct streams.
legacy: Both streams were alive in 2010. The Disciples' ecumenical commitment was institutional — they were founding members of both the Federal Council in 1908 and the World Council in 1948 — which is what their founding plea for unity became; the independent Christian Churches remained a large, congregationally governed stream. The irony was not lost on either of them: a movement founded to end division had divided twice.

relationsSummary: This is the twentieth-century continuation of the Black church tradition. The Great Migration remade it as an urban, northern institution; the Church of God in Christ rose from 1907; the National Baptist Convention split in 1915; the civil rights movement grew out of these congregations, with Martin Luther King Jr and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, founded in 1957; and James Cone's writings opened the field of Black theology. Its worship traditions also share roots with the Pentecostal movement that grew out of the Azusa Street revival.
why: The Great Migration carried Black congregations out of the rural South and into northern cities, remaking a whole religious culture within a generation; the Church of God in Christ took its Pentecostal turn out of Memphis in 1907 and grew into one of the century's major denominations, while the National Baptist Convention split in 1915. From the 1950s these congregations were the civil rights movement's infrastructure — Martin Luther King Jr. worked out of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, founded in 1957 — and at the end of the 1960s James Cone's books opened Black theology as a field of its own.
legacy: In 2010 it was a living tradition, and one of the great Christian stories of the twentieth century. It gave the civil-rights movement its buildings, its money, its networks and much of its language. Through the century, the sermon was where much of America's public moral argument got made. Black theology became a field with its own books and its own critics. And it carried forward the Black church of the nineteenth century, whose congregations became the civil-rights church of this one.

statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: This renewal is the North Atlantic middle. Behind it lay the early Pentecostal movement, which had mostly settled by the 1920s. Ahead lay the Global South Pentecostal explosion, from the 1950s on. Its usual starting point is Dennis Bennett's announcement in Van Nuys on 3 April 1960. Then came the charismatic wave in the mainline churches, Calvary Chapel in 1965 and the Jesus movement of 1967 to 1972. The Vineyard association of 1982 began the third wave. Calvary Chapel and the Vineyard built big new churches, of a kind some writers called megachurches. How far the seeker megachurches and the New Calvinist networks drew on this renewal is less clear. The Word of Faith movement grew in the same years. Kenneth Hagin's Rhema Bible Training Center dates from 1974. The renewal itself faded as a wave, but the bodies it made lived on and are named here.
why: On 3 April 1960 Dennis Bennett told his Van Nuys, California congregation that he had spoken in tongues, an announcement conventionally marking the start of a charismatic movement that spread through mainline Protestant parishes without most of their members ever leaving. Alongside it, the Jesus movement of 1967 to 1972 reached young people outside any church, finding its best-known home at Calvary Chapel, founded in 1965, before the wave handed on to the newly formed Vineyard association in 1982.
legacy: The wave faded, but the bodies it created did not. In 2010 Calvary Chapel and the Vineyard were still active, with churches worldwide. Its longest effect was probably musical. Chuck Smith of Calvary Chapel founded Maranatha! Music in 1971. Larry Eskridge's history of the Jesus People gives Jesus music a chapter. The worship style of the Jesus movement spread through a very large part of English-speaking Protestantism. It spread whether or not the singers knew where it came from. What else the renewal planted is harder to judge. The megachurches and the church-planting networks of the 2000s may have grown in ground it had turned over. That debt has not been shown directly. Roman Catholics shared in the same renewal. A Presbyterian report of 1969 already counted them in it.

statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: The World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh in 1910 set three streams running. The International Missionary Council began in 1921, Life and Work in 1925, and Faith and Order in 1927. These came together in the World Council of Churches, formed at Amsterdam in 1948. The missionary council joined it at New Delhi in 1961. Orthodox churches were members. In 1920 the Ecumenical Patriarchate had called for a fellowship of churches. The Roman Catholic Church did not join. In 1928 Pope Pius XI ruled that Catholics could not take part. After the Second Vatican Council, Rome worked with it. In its first years most of its member churches were Protestant and Western. It may have grown in part out of the world of the mainline churches, but the evidence for that is thin. The Lausanne movement of 1974 gave an evangelical answer to the same question. How should divided churches work together? In Africa, churches formed the All Africa Conference of Churches. It was founded at its first assembly in Kampala on 20 April 1963. A meeting at Ibadan in 1958 came first. In 1971 the Kenyan theologian John Gatu first called for a moratorium on missionaries. The conference's third assembly met at Lusaka in May 1974.
why: The World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh in 1910 left three currents running. One was the International Missionary Council, founded in 1921. The other two were the Life and Work and Faith and Order movements of the 1920s. They came together in the World Council of Churches, formed at Amsterdam in 1948 with 147 member churches. The missionary council joined at New Delhi in 1961. It was a council of churches, not a church. It had no power over its members and no creed of its own. Orthodox churches belonged to it. The Roman Catholic Church never joined. In 1928 Pius XI ruled that Catholics could not take part. After the Second Vatican Council, Rome worked alongside it.
legacy: In 2010 it was a living body. For a century it had been the main attempt to get divided churches to act and argue together in one room. Its assemblies and its Faith and Order work produced many shared statements. They dealt with questions that had split churches for centuries, and its member churches used them. This map draws it as the counter-pole to the Lausanne movement of 1974. They are two answers, from the same century, to one question: how should churches that disagree work together? It was also one home of the mainline century, which may have helped to build it.

relationsSummary: The modernist crisis — condemned in the 1907 decree Lamentabili and encyclical Pascendi, and enforced by an anti-modernist oath from 1910, targeting scholars like Alfred Loisy and George Tyrrell — ran the same argument over history, scripture, and doctrine inside Catholicism a generation before it split American Protestantism. Divino Afflante Spiritu in 1943 reopened the biblical scholarship Pascendi had closed, and the worker-priest movement and the nouvelle théologie became the seedbed for the Second Vatican Council. Opus Dei, founded in 1928, and other new lay movements also trace their origins to this period. The period runs up to the eve of the council in 1962.
why: In 1907 Rome condemned what it called modernism in the decree Lamentabili and the encyclical Pascendi, targeting scholars like Alfred Loisy and George Tyrrell, and required an anti-modernist oath of clergy from 1910 — the same argument over history, scripture and doctrine that would split American Protestantism a generation later. The reversal came slowly: Divino Afflante Spiritu in 1943 reopened the biblical scholarship Pascendi had closed, and the worker-priest experiment and the nouvelle théologie's return to the church fathers became the seedbed the Second Vatican Council would build on.
legacy: The church is the same church, and this half-century is a chapter in its life rather than a movement that ended: it runs to the eve of the council in 1962 and hands straight on. What this period left behind is the council itself. Almost everything the Second Vatican Council did had been prepared in these decades — the biblical scholarship released in 1943, the liturgical movement, the return to the church fathers, and the questions the worker-priests raised about where the church actually is.

statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: This is a largely gentile movement of Torah observance. It is distinct from Messianic Judaism, a movement of Jewish believers, and both sides drew that line in their own writing. It took shape through Torah study groups, congregations that kept the Sabbath and the feasts, and teaching ministries online. Its clearest root is a newer wave linked to First Fruits of Zion, founded in 1992. The Sacred Name movement of the 1930s kept the Sabbath and the feasts long before. How far the newer current drew on it is not clear.
why: From the 1990s a largely gentile current of Christians took up Torah observance. They kept the Sabbath and the biblical feasts in congregations and, more and more, through teaching online. Its own writers took care to set it apart from Messianic Judaism, a movement of Jewish believers. Its best-documented body, First Fruits of Zion, was founded in 1992. In 2009 it published a public shift away from teaching 'One Law' toward what it called Divine Invitation. The movement's One-Law side answered in print. An older current, the Sacred Name movement of the 1930s, also kept the Sabbath and the feasts. Its magazine The Faith dates from 1937. How far the newer current drew on it is not clear.
legacy: In 2010 this was a current in progress rather than a settled tradition, and this map says so. Institutionally it was thin — a handful of publishers and congregational networks, and a great deal of video — which makes it genuinely hard to describe: no central body, no shared confession, and no independent count of any kind, so every figure in circulation comes from self-report or journalism. What it did was put a question back into ordinary Christian conversation that most churches had long considered settled: what, if anything, the Torah asks of gentile believers. Its individual bodies differ widely from one another, and the map assesses them one at a time.

statusDescription: Tiered deferred on a smaller frame (Tier 3). It was a political movement carried by organizations, not a church or a confession. Its public record is moderate to rich. What it formed in people's lives beyond politics is thinly recorded, and this entry says so.

They were the Moral Majority (1979–1989), the Christian Coalition (from 1989) and the Faith and Freedom Coalition (from 2009).
why: In June 1979 Jerry Falwell and four other ministers founded the Moral Majority. In August 1980 Ronald Reagan, then running for president, spoke at a briefing in Dallas. Another group, the Religious Roundtable, ran it. He said the gathering was nonpartisan, so it could not endorse him. Then he added, 'I endorse you and what you're doing.' The Moral Majority closed in 1989, and Pat Robertson founded the Christian Coalition that year. In 2009 Ralph Reed, the Christian Coalition's first executive director, founded the Faith and Freedom Coalition.
legacy: Its groups changed over thirty years, but the movement carried on. In 2010 the historian Daniel K. Williams told its story in God's Own Party. The record shows its political work well. It shows much less of what the movement meant for its members' faith.

The Church of Alexandria and Miaphysite Egypt

statusDescription: Not yet researched or tiered; added so that works in the Library have a place on the Atlas.
relationsSummary: A rival church to the bishops of Alexandria from about 306. It broke with them, and its members brought charges against Athanasius. The Council of Nicaea tried to settle the split in 325. Antony of the desert would hold no communion with it.
why: A quarrel between two bishops in a time of persecution split the church of Egypt for more than two centuries. The Melitians kept their own bishops, priests and monks. They fought Athanasius before councils and emperors. Their letters, in Greek and Coptic, let them speak for themselves.
legacy: No church today descends from the Melitians. Their papyri give something rare: the losing side of an early church quarrel, in its own words. Most of what is known of such groups comes only from their enemies. The letters also show an organized community of Egyptian monks in the 330s, outside the main church.

name: The Luciferians
statusDescription: Proposed for later study. Not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: They began as the hardest of the Nicene party. Lucifer wrote against the emperor Constantius and the bishops who took his creed. In 362 the church agreed to let bishops who had given way keep their sees. Lucifer's followers would not accept them, and stood apart. Jerome wrote a dialogue against them, and Augustine said they had cut themselves off. In 383 or 384 two of their priests asked the emperors for protection, and the emperors granted it.
why: In 359 almost every bishop of the West signed a creed the emperor wanted. Later most of them took it back. The church then let them keep their places. A small party said no. A bishop who had given way once, they held, could never lead the church again. Their stand shows how hard it was to heal the church after the fights over the creed. It also left the losing side's case in its own words.
legacy:
The group did not last, but its case lives on in its own words. Its petition was kept in a Roman book of letters from emperors and popes, the Collectio Avellana. Lucifer's pamphlets survive whole. Jerome's dialogue against the group holds his famous line on the council of Ariminum: the whole world groaned to find itself Arian.

The quarrel also raised an older question, which Jerome traces back to Cyprian. Should people baptized outside the church be baptized again when they come in?

name: The Carthusians — The Later Medieval Charterhouses
statusDescription: Proposed for later study. Not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: The same order as the first Carthusians, still keeping its old rule of the cell. In England its monks copied and kept the books of the English mystics, The Cloud of Unknowing and Walter Hilton's Scale of Perfection. Nicholas Love, prior of Mount Grace, attacked the Lollards in his life of Christ. In the Low Countries a Carthusian prior turned Geert Grote's life around, and Grote went on to found the New Devotion.
why: The Carthusians lived alone in their cells, but they read and copied a great deal. In England they became keepers of the new books of prayer written in English. Their scribes copied The Cloud of Unknowing and Hilton's Scale of Perfection, wrote notes in them and passed them on. One of their priors put the life of Christ into plain English for readers who knew no Latin. Modern editors of the Cloud and the Scale still lean on copies made in their houses.
legacy:
The care of these houses still shapes how the English mystics are read. Evelyn Underhill based her 1923 edition of Hilton's Scale on the London Charterhouse copy. Justin McCann checked his 1924 text of the Cloud against the Latin version made at Mount Grace. Love's Mirror was copied again and again; its 1908 editor knew of twenty-three manuscripts. When the English houses fell under Henry VIII, some of the books are said to have gone with the monks into exile.

The end came in the 1530s, when Henry VIII made himself head of the church in England. In May 1535 John Houghton, prior of the London Charterhouse, was hanged at Tyburn with the priors of Beauvale and Axholme. Many of their brothers followed them to the scaffold or died in Newgate prison, and some escaped to found an English charterhouse at Bruges.

name: Mission-Born Christianity in New France

livingEvidence.basis: The Library's last word is the move of about three hundred Huron Christians to Quebec in 1650. No text in the repo traces a church descended from them after that year.

statusDescription: The Jesuits' yearly Relations are in hand, in French and English, to 1650. The converts speak in them only as the missionaries wrote them down; no text in a convert's own hand is in the Library yet. Not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: Grew from the Jesuit mission to New France. Near Quebec, Algonquin families settled at Sillery from 1638, and most became Christians. Far to the west, the Jesuits worked among the Hurons. When war with the Iroquois broke the Huron nation, about three hundred Christian Hurons went down to Quebec in 1650.
why: Here the converts' words survive, though only in the priests' reports. At Sillery, Christian families met at night without the Jesuits and made rules of their own. Among the Hurons, a convert named Joseph Chihwatenhwa taught his people like an elder brother. In 1650 the last Huron Christians asked to be led to Quebec, so that their faith would not die out.
legacy: The Library's record of this church stops in 1650. A year before, the Jesuits counted more than three thousand people baptized among the Hurons. The few hundred who reached Quebec had lost their homes and their kin. The Jesuit who led them wrote that they "have not lost their faith." What became of their church after 1650 is not yet told from the Library.

name: The Swedish Lutherans of New Sweden
statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed. Thin: one source, Acrelius (1759).
relationsSummary: Sweden planted a colony on the Delaware in 1638, with a Swedish pastor. After Swedish rule ended in 1655, few pastors were left. In 1693 the people wrote home to beg for ministers and books. From 1697 the king and archbishop of Sweden sent pastors again. In the 1740s the churches shut out Moravian preachers. Their provost Acrelius visited the cloister at Ephrata in 1753 and argued with its brothers.
why: A small Swedish people on an American river kept their Lutheran church for more than a century. For years they had no pastor of their own tongue. Laymen read sermons from a book in the churches. In 1693 they wrote to Sweden in their own words, for "two Swedish ministers" and two hundred catechisms. Sweden answered, and went on sending pastors for nearly ninety years.
legacy: From 1696 to 1786, Sweden sent twenty-four pastors to the churches on the Delaware. The crown paid for their voyages out and home. In time the Swedish language died out among the settlers' children. Then Sweden stopped sending pastors. What became of the congregations after that is not yet told from the Library.

name: English Unitarianism

livingEvidence.basis: The Library carries the Essex Street chapel to Belsham's account of 1812 and the law of 1813. No later text in the repo traces today's British Unitarian churches back to it.

otherLinksToLivingEntries.otherName: Anti-Trinitarian Currents (Servetus; Polish Brethren/Socinians; Transylvanian Unitarians)

statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, as a register entry. By its own founding sermon and writings, it reads as stepping outside the doctrinal floor. The question is not decided yet. Not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: Theophilus Lindsey left the Church of England. In 1774 he opened his own chapel in London. Joseph Priestley came to it from the old Dissenting churches. There he had moved from Arian to Unitarian belief. Earlier English writers took up the ideas of Socinus and the Polish Brethren. The evidence for that link is thin. Lindsey's prayer book shaped the first Unitarian liturgy in Boston. Priestley argued in print with the new Swedenborgian church in Birmingham. One of its leaders answered him.
why: In 1774 a clergyman who had left the Church of England opened a chapel in London. Its people met, he said, as "a separate congregation", so that they might worship God alone. Joseph Priestley, chemist and Dissenting minister, defended the same belief in print each year. In 1791 a mob burned his meeting house and his home in Birmingham. In 1813 the law at last gave Unitarians the same rights as other Dissenters.
legacy: For years Unitarians stood outside the law that protected other Dissenters. In 1813 they were given the same rights. By then the chapel's books were read far from London. In 1810 a small society in New York State read sermons by Lindsey, Priestley and Toulmin when it had no minister. The story of the English churches after 1813 is not yet told from the Library.

name: The Hutterite Brethren

livingEvidence.basis: A living tradition whose own chronicle travels with it. Beck (1883) traces the families from Hungary to Russia, and to a colony near the Sea of Azov from 1852. Wolkan's preface (1923) says the Brethren who left Russia for America in 1874 still held the chronicle, and their colony in Alberta published it. Nothing later is in the Library.

statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: The Hutterites grew out of the Anabaptist church at Nikolsburg in 1528. Habsburg rulers hunted them. They burned Jakob Hutter in 1536. In 1622 they drove the Brethren out of Moravia. From 1757 the government in Hungary broke up the last of their homes. A few families kept the faith and moved on to Russia.
why: In 1528 a band of Anabaptists left Nikolsburg in Moravia. On the road their leaders spread a cloak on the ground. Everyone laid down their goods on it, freely and unforced. From that act came a church that held all its goods in common. It took its name from Jakob Hutter, burned in 1536. Its own chronicle tells the story from the inside.
legacy: The Brethren never let their chronicle go. Beck found their families in Russia, near the Sea of Azov, by 1852. In 1874 the Brethren moved from Russia to America and took the book with them. In 1923 the Hutterian Brethren in Canada published it, as a house book for every member.

name: The Mennonites and the Amish

livingEvidence.basis: The church's own prefaces claim the martyrs as its forebears, from van Braght (1659) to the English edition of 1886. The grade Documented covers the Mennonite line. The Amish descent is shown only by one mention, in the Elkhart manual of 1890, pending the source pass. The Amish division of the 1690s is not yet in the Library, and no inside text after 1890 is.

statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, carrying forward part of an earlier entry; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: These churches were heirs of the Swiss and Dutch Anabaptists. The Mennonites of Pennsylvania asked the Ephrata Brethren to print their book of martyrs in German. A church manual of 1890 tells of Amish churches too.
why: After 1650 the heirs of the Anabaptists became settled churches. In 1660 Thieleman van Braght of Dordrecht gathered their martyrs into one great book, the Martyrs Mirror. He longed to be like "my slain fellow brethren and sisters". The book crossed the sea with his people. In Pennsylvania the Ephrata Brethren printed it in German, and in 1886 an English edition came out.
legacy: The martyr book still speaks for these churches. In 1886 its publishers called the martyrs "especially precious to us, as Mennonites". Through them, they wrote, God handed down what "we hold and practice at the present day". The churches live on, but the Library does not yet hold their story after 1890.

name: The Melkite Greek Catholic Church after 1815

livingEvidence.basis: The same see and the same line of patriarchs. The synod of 1816 chose a successor to Macarius Tauil. Charon (1910-1911) names Cyril VIII Geha, elected in 1902, as the patriarch of his own day. Nothing after 1911 is in the Library.

otherLinksToLivingEntries.otherName: The Catholic Church of the Long Nineteenth Century

statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
relationsSummary: This is the church of the 1724 split at Antioch, carried on by the same line of patriarchs. It stayed in communion with Rome. In 1831 Rome's mission office called its bishops together in synod. In 1848 a decree of the sultan gave it a civil standing of its own.
why: In the nineteenth century the Melkite Catholics won a place of their own. Their bishops met again and again in synod to choose patriarchs. Maximos III Mazloum, patriarch from 1833 to 1855, won a decree from the sultan in 1848. From then on, Cyril Charon wrote in 1910, the Melkite Catholics were fully free in civil matters.
legacy: The civil standing won in 1848 lasted. Writing in 1910, Charon says it still held in his day. Through these years the bishops chose each patriarch in synod, and Rome then confirmed him. The church lives on, but the Library does not yet hold its story after 1911.
